cards.title: Normal chat
cards.blurb: A quick, conversational explanation with no tools involved.
cards.prompt: /chat Explain nuclear spin hyperpolarisation to a biophysics PhD student in three short paragraphs: what it is, why it matters for studying proteins and membranes, and its main limitation.

cards.title: Ask our papers
cards.blurb: Answers from hyperpolarisation papers uploaded by consortium members, with citations.
cards.prompt: /research Using my uploaded papers, compare optical and microwave-driven routes to nuclear spin hyperpolarisation. Cite the papers you use.

cards.title: Compute and plot
cards.blurb: Writes and runs Python, then delivers the figure as an artifact.
cards.prompt: /code Write and run Python that computes the thermal 13C polarisation at 9.4 T and 298 K, then plots the decay of a hyperpolarised 13C sample starting at 20% polarisation with T1 = 60 s against that thermal level, on a log axis. Show the plot.

cards.title: It won't invent a paper
cards.blurb: We ask about a paper that doesn't exist. Watch it look, then say so.
cards.prompt: /research Summarise the main findings of "Cryogen-free parahydrogen relay hyperpolarisation of intact GPCRs in living yeast at 1 T" by Lindqvist, Okafor and Brandt (Nature Biophysics, 2021).

cards.title: Deep Research
cards.blurb: Plans, searches, reads and writes a cited report, in the background.
cards.prompt: How do optical and microwave DNP compare for room-temperature hyperpolarisation, and what are the prospects for biomolecules?
